title: Fear not
hook: fear not appears again and again in scripture

segments.voice: Yesterday, wounded healers: comfort received becomes comfort given, and the risen Jesus shows his hands and feet. Your line was wounds that heal. Who got your short message? Day one thousand three hundred ninety-eight.

Abram, in a vision, childless and waiting. A young woman in Nazareth, with an angel in the room. Shepherds in a dark field, suddenly lit up. Women at a tomb that should not be empty. John on the island of Patmos, falling at someone's feet as though dead. Different places, different stories, different people. And to each of them, heaven says the same two words. Fear not. Today: fear not.

Listen to what comes right after those words. To Abram: "Fear not, Abram: I am thy shield, and thy exceeding great reward." To Mary: "Fear not, Mary: for thou hast found favour with God." To the shepherds: "Fear not: for, behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people." To John on Patmos, with a right hand laid on him: "Fear not; I am the first and the last." And through the prophet Isaiah, to Israel, called my servant: "Fear thou not; for I am with thee: be not dismayed; for I am thy God." Hear the pattern? For. I am. Behold. In these passages, fear not is never just a command left hanging. It's a sentence with a second half, and the second half is a reason, usually a presence. Next, notice that the frightened people aren't scolded. Luke says the shepherds were "sore afraid." The angel doesn't tell them they're overreacting. It gives them news big enough to step out of the fear. Then notice when the words come. Abram is waiting on a promise. Mary is about to say yes to something enormous. The women at the tomb are standing at the edge of a story that's just changed. Fear not keeps showing up at thresholds, right before something new. So in scripture, fear not doesn't pretend fear isn't there. It speaks to the fear directly, and then it gives a reason.
screen: `FEAR NOT, ABRAM: I AM THY SHIELD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say fear not to one fear. Settle, and breathe. Let one fear come up: about money, your health, a person you love, what's coming next. Don't argue with it. Just name it plainly. Then say the two words to it, out loud or inside: fear not. And give it a second half, the way scripture does. If you pray, you can borrow Isaiah's: for I am with thee. If you don't, let the second half be something true and steady: I'm breathing, I'm here, this moment holds. The bell holds the time.
Fear not. Heaven's words to Abram, Mary, the shepherds and John, each time followed by a reason: I am, for, behold.
Your line: fear not. Today, when a fear rises, finish the sentence the way scripture does: fear not, for, and then one true thing. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: Christians often memorize fear-not verses such as Isaiah 41:10 and say them in anxious moments, and the angel's 'fear not' to the shepherds is read aloud in churches at Christmas.
